Latin suescere 'to accustom'). In English from c. 1600 as 'companionship, fellowship'; later a religious guild; the anthropological sense dates from Service.
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Defined against kinship: a sodality is precisely not a lineage or clan. In the theological usage, whether denominations count is disputed: Wikipedia's 'Modality (theology)' lists schools of theology, orders, monasteries and convents as sodalities but calls denominations arguably modalities.
fields.WN_Gloss: people engaged in a particular occupation

fields.Received_Definition: A panoramic painting on the inner wall of a cylindrical room or rotunda, viewed from a central platform so that it surrounds the spectator 360°, often with a three-dimensional foreground ('faux terrain') blending into the canvas; also the building that houses it. In the US the word distinguished the circular panorama from the moving panorama; famous survivors include the Gettysburg (Philippoteaux, 1883) and Atlanta cycloramas and the Racławice Panorama.
fields.Etymology: cyclo- (Greek kyklos 'circle, wheel', PIE *kwel-) + -rama, abstracted from panorama (Greek horama 'sight, spectacle'). First attested 1840 as a circular panorama in a cylindrical room. The format descends from Robert Barker's panorama (Edinburgh, 1787).
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Often used interchangeably with panorama, though panorama names the wide image and cyclorama its display in the round. In theatre the word now means a curved backdrop or sky-cloth, a separate sense.
fields.WN_Gloss: a picture (or series of pictures) representing a continuous scene

fields.My_Definition:
homo economicus (ˌɛkəˈnɒmɪkəs)
n
a theoretical human being who rationally calculates the costs and benefits of every action before making a decision, used as the basis for a number of economic theories and models
fields.Received_Definition: 'Economic man': the model of the human agent as consistently rational and narrowly self-interested, pursuing given ends as efficiently as possible; the rationality is one of means, not of the wisdom of the ends. It descends from J. S. Mill's abstraction of man as 'a being who desires to possess wealth' (1836) and underlies neoclassical and rational-choice economics.
fields.Etymology: New Latin homo 'man, human being' + oeconomicus 'economic' (from Greek oikonomikos, oikos 'house' + nomos 'law, management'). The English 'economic man' arose in the late 19th c. among critics of Mill (J. K. Ingram, A History of Political Economy, 1888); the Latin form appears in C. S. Devas, The Groundwork of Economics (1883), and is often traced to Pareto (1906).
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Contested as description versus method: critics from Simon (bounded rationality) and Kahneman–Tversky to Sen, Polanyi and feminist economists attack it as a picture of human nature, while defenders treat it as a deliberate methodological fiction (Caruso's methodological vs anthropological homo economicus). Also spelled homo oeconomicus.
fields.WN_Gloss: any living or extinct member of the family Hominidae characterized by superior intelligence, articulate speech, and erect carriage

fields.Received_Definition: Latin form of obol: a small silver coin of ancient Greece worth one sixth of a drachma, and the corresponding unit of weight (about 0.72 g). By extension, a trifling sum; the coin placed with the dead to pay Charon's ferry fare.
fields.Etymology: Latin obolus, from Greek obolos (ὀβολός), identical with obelos 'spit, spike, nail; bar of metal used as money', recalling early iron spits traded by weight (six to a handful, a drachma). Origin of obelos uncertain, possibly Pre-Greek (Beekes). In English since the 1660s as obol; Middle English obolus for a small weight and 'ob' for a halfpenny.
fields.WN_Gloss: Not in this sense. WordNet has only the unit of weight (oewn-13740556-n: a Greek unit of weight equal to one tenth of a gram); the coin sense is missing.

fields.Received_Definition: Ancient Greek adjective (ἀποκηρύξιμος, -ον), "to be sold by public auction"; LSJ records it under ἀποκήρυκτος with an epigraphic citation (IG 2.476). It belongs to the ἀποκηρύσσω family, whose senses split between selling by herald's proclamation (auction) and publicly renouncing or disowning (a son, a claim).
fields.Etymology: From Greek ἀπό (off, away) + κηρύσσω (to proclaim as a herald, from κῆρυξ, herald) + -ιμος (adjective suffix: fit for, liable to). The verb's 'auction' and 'renounce/disinherit' senses both come from public proclamation.
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Not to be confused with ἀποκήρυκτος, 'publicly renounced, disinherited'; the -ιμος form is attested in the auction sense only.

fields.My_Definition:
mu·ta·gen  (myo͞o′tə-jən, -jĕn′)
n.
An agent, such as a chemical, ultraviolet light, or a radioactive element, that can induce or increase the frequency of mutation in an organism.
fields.Received_Definition: The capacity of a physical, chemical or biological agent to induce permanent, transmissible changes in the amount or structure of an organism's genetic material, or to raise the rate of such mutation. Measured in toxicology by assays such as the bacterial Ames test (OECD 471).
fields.Etymology: mutagen (1946, 'agent that causes mutation': mutation, from Latin mutare 'to change', + -gen, via French -gène from Greek -genēs 'born, produced') + -ic + -ity.
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Narrower than genotoxicity: all mutagens are genotoxic, but not all genotoxic agents are mutagenic (DNA damage that is repaired or not heritable does not count).
fields.WN_Gloss: capable of inducing mutation (used mainly of extracellular factors such as X-rays or chemical pollution)

fields.Received_Definition: Transitive verb: to endow or imbue with a soul; to put a soul into a body or thing. The noun ensoulment names the moment or act of a being's receiving a soul, a long-running question in Aristotelian, Christian, Jewish, Islamic and other traditions.
fields.Etymology: en- (to put into, from Old French/Latin in-) + soul (Old English sāwol, Proto-Germanic *saiwalō). First known use 1605 (Merriam-Webster).
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Close to 'animate', but ensoul names the giving of a soul rather than of motion or life; when ensoulment happens (conception, quickening, birth) is a contested question, notably Aristotle's and Aquinas's delayed ensoulment against ensoulment at conception.

fields.Received_Definition: Not involving causation or not arising from a cause. Its best-known technical use is C. G. Jung's 'Synchronicity: An Acausal Connecting Principle' (Eranos lecture 1951; with Wolfgang Pauli), where it names a connection between inner and outer events made by meaningful coincidence rather than by cause and effect.
fields.Etymology: a- (not, from Greek privative a-) + causal (from Latin causa). First known use 1908 (Merriam-Webster).
fields.Boundary_Tensions: In Jung, 'acausal' does not mean random or unrelated: it claims a relation by meaning that sits outside the causal order, which is why the concept is contested by empiricists.
fields.WN_Gloss: Not in WordNet. Only the base 'causal' is present (oewn-00324097-s: involving or constituting a cause; causing).

fields.Received_Definition: In grammar, a change in the form of a word (usually an ending) that marks a grammatical category such as tense, case, number or person; more broadly, a bending or modulation (of a line, or of the voice). In Deleuze's The Fold: Leibniz and the Baroque (1988), inflection is the genetic element of the fold: the point at which a curve changes direction, from which series, the objectile and the point of view are derived.
fields.Etymology: From Latin inflexio (a bending, modification), from inflectere (to bend in, curve; fig. to change), from in- + flectere (to bend). English early 15c. (also inflexion); vocal sense c. 1600; grammatical sense 1660s.
fields.Boundary_Tensions: The grammatical sense (morphological change of a word) and the geometric/Deleuzian sense (change of curvature) share only the image of bending; grammar-based readings miss the Baroque use.
fields.WN_Gloss: a change in the form of a word (usually by adding a suffix) to indicate a change in its grammatical function

fields.Received_Definition: Having windows, or perforated with one or more small openings or pores; used in architecture (fenestration, the arrangement of windows) and in anatomy and medicine (fenestrated capillaries, a fenestrated catheter).
fields.Etymology: From Latin fenestra (window, opening for light), perhaps from Etruscan; via fenestrare. Architectural 'fenestration' 1846, anatomical 1870; 'fenestrated' first known use c. 1852 (Merriam-Webster).
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Inverts Leibniz: the monad 'has no windows through which anything could enter or leave' (Monadology §7), which Deleuze reads as the windowless upper floor of the Baroque house above the windowed lower floor.

fields.Received_Definition: Of, relating to or consisting of monads: simple, indivisible, self-contained units. Philosophically tied to Leibniz's Monadology (1714), where monads are windowless simple substances that perceive the whole world from their own point of view. In logic, a predicate or relation taking a single argument ('x is red').
fields.Etymology: From monad + -ic. Monad: Late Latin monas (gen. monadis), from Greek monas (unit), from monos (alone). English 1610s 'unit'; metaphysical sense 1748, Leibniz apparently taking the word from Giordano Bruno.
fields.Boundary_Tensions: The logical sense (one-place predicate) and the functional-programming 'monad' are unrelated to Leibnizian metaphysics despite the shared word.

fields.Received_Definition: The frame through which an audience views a stage: in the modern theatre, the wall and arch separating stage from auditorium (or the apron in front of the curtain); in Hellenistic Greek theatres, the proskenion, a narrow raised stage for actors. The proscenium plane is effectively the 'fourth wall'.
fields.Etymology: From Latin proscaenium, from Greek proskēnion (space in front of the scenery), from pro- (in front) + skēnē (tent, booth, stage; source of 'scene'). English c. 1600 for the ancient stage; figurative 'foreground' 1640s; modern sense 1807.
fields.Boundary_Tensions: Ambiguous between the arch/wall that frames and the apron in front of the curtain; the Teatro Farnese (1618) is the earliest surviving true proscenium arch, the Teatro Olimpico (1585) is often wrongly cited.
fields.WN_Gloss: the wall that separates the stage from the auditorium in a modern theater

fields.Received_Definition: In lexicography and morphology, the canonical or citation form chosen to represent a lexeme, and the headword under which a dictionary entry is filed (break for breaks, broke, broken). In mathematics and logic, a subsidiary proposition proved or assumed in order to prove another.
fields.Etymology: From Greek lēmma (pl. lēmmata), 'something received or taken; an argument; something taken for granted', from lambanein (to take). English 1560s, in mathematics. Same root as dilemma.
fields.Boundary_Tensions: The lexicographic lemma (headword) and the mathematical lemma (auxiliary proposition) share the root sense of 'something taken' but are distinct technical uses.
fields.WN_Gloss: the heading that indicates the subject of an annotation or a literary composition or a dictionary entry

fields.Received_Definition: Marcel Broodthaers (1924–1976), Belgian poet, filmmaker and visual artist associated with institutional critique. After some twenty years as a poet he turned to art in 1963–64 by setting unsold copies of his book Pense-Bête in plaster; later founded the fictional Musée d'Art Moderne, Département des Aigles (from 1968). His Un coup de dés jamais n'abolira le hasard: Image (1969) keeps Mallarmé's layout but covers every line with black bars, replacing 'poème' with 'image'.

A manuscript page, usually parchment, scraped or washed so it could be reused, with traces of the earlier writing still visible beneath the new. Figuratively, any surface or structure in which successive layers remain legible through one another; De Quincey applied it to memory: 'What else than a natural and mighty palimpsest is the human brain?' (Suspiria de Profundis, 1845).
fields.Etymology: From Latin palimpsestus, from Greek palimpsēstos (scraped again), from palin (again) + psēn (to rub smooth). English 1660s.
fields.WN_Gloss: a manuscript (usually written on papyrus or parchment) on which more than one text has been written with the earlier writing incompletely erased and still visible
